speaker: Mike Krieger
title: Anthropic's CPO on what comes next | Mike Krieger
question: In AI products, why do open integration protocols unlock ecosystem adoption where bespoke integrations fail?
guest: My equation for the utility of AI products has three parts: model intelligence, context and memory, and applications and UI. You need all three to converge, and having the right internal context from tools like Slack or Google Drive is often the entire difference between a good answer and a bad answer. When we started building integrations, we found we were rebuilding every single one from scratch in a non-repeatable way. So two of our engineers asked: what if we made this an open protocol so people could build integrations once and use them across Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini? It is the classic commoditize your complements strategy. We are building models, not an integrations company, and as a challenger, third parties will not build exclusive integrations just for us out of the gate. An open protocol inverted that so it did not feel like wasted work. Going forward, exposing every product primitive via a protocol lets agents read and write back directly. Compared to computer use, which has many limitations, protocol-exposed primitives make everything scriptable, composable, and usable agentically by models.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Open protocols win because they change the economics of integration from multiplicative to additive. With bespoke integrations, every AI application must build a custom connector to every tool or data source, an M×N problem where each connector is costly to build, breaks when either side changes, and benefits only one pairing. An open protocol such as the Model Context Protocol turns this into M+N: a tool vendor implements the standard once and works with every compliant AI client, and each client gains access to every existing server.

That shift creates network effects. Each new server makes every client more valuable and vice versa, so adoption compounds rather than stalling at whatever integrations one vendor can afford to maintain. Openness also matters in its own right: third parties will invest in a neutral standard because they are not locked into a single vendor's roadmap, and the long tail of niche tools gets built by the people who know them best rather than waiting on the platform owner's priorities. Shared conventions for discovery, authentication and security also reduce the trust and maintenance burden for everyone.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Bespoke integrations trap AI products in an N-by-M scaling bottleneck: every AI host or agent must build, secure, and maintain custom connectors for every external data source and tool. Because useful AI depends on live context and reliable action execution across fragmented software stacks, maintaining brittle, one-off glue code quickly overwhelms engineering teams as APIs, schemas, and authentication models evolve.

Open integration protocols, such as the Model Context Protocol, collapse that matrix into an N-plus-M architecture. Service providers expose a single standardized interface once and become immediately usable across every compliant AI client, while AI applications instantly tap into a shared, growing catalog of capabilities. Open protocols also standardize AI-native primitives, including dynamic tool discovery, structured context exchange, and explicit authorization boundaries, eliminating the security and reliability inconsistencies of ad-hoc wrappers. By preventing vendor lock-in and driving marginal integration costs toward zero, open standards ignite two-sided network effects: third-party developers invest knowing their integrations are portable, turning isolated AI products into a composable ecosystem.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer: Open protocols turn an N×M integration problem into N+M. With bespoke integrations, every AI app has to build and maintain its own connector to every tool, data source, or service. Each one is a one-off cost, it breaks whenever either side changes, and it only pays off for a single pairing. So only the biggest platforms get supported, and the long tail never shows up. A shared protocol like Anthropic's Model Context Protocol (MCP) changes this. A tool vendor writes one server and it works with every compatible client, and a client gets every existing server for free. That creates network effects: each new participant makes the protocol more valuable for everyone else, so adoption builds on itself rather than stalling. Openness also lowers trust and lock-in risk. Competitors such as OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft can adopt a neutral standard without strengthening a rival's proprietary moat, and developers can build on it knowing their work won't be stranded. Standard interfaces also make shared security practices, tooling, registries, and documentation possible, which bespoke integrations can't support. The web's HTTP and the Language Server Protocol for code editors followed the same pattern.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Bespoke integrations trap AI ecosystems in an M×N scaling problem: every AI application must build and maintain custom connectors for every external tool and data source, while every software vendor must duplicate work for each AI platform. Because AI products and APIs evolve rapidly, this one-off glue code becomes fragile, expensive to maintain, and slow to ship.

Open integration protocols collapse that complexity into an M+N model by standardizing how AI systems discover capabilities, authenticate, pass context, and invoke actions. Tool builders can implement a protocol once and immediately become accessible across all compliant AI clients, while AI products gain instant access to a growing catalog of integrations without writing custom adapters.

Just as importantly, open standards reduce vendor lock-in. Enterprises and third-party developers are far more willing to invest engineering effort—and establish consistent security, permissioning, and observability controls—when their integrations remain portable across models and vendors. That shared foundation creates self-reinforcing network effects that proprietary connectors rarely achieve.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Open integration protocols let a tool provider build one integration that works across compatible AI products, and let each AI product support many tools through a common interface. Bespoke integrations repeat much of that work for every product–tool pair, including agreeing on how to discover capabilities, pass inputs, and handle errors. That cost makes it hard to justify supporting smaller products or niche tools.

A shared protocol also lets developers ship integrations without waiting for each AI vendor to prioritize a partnership. As more products adopt the protocol, a single integration reaches more users. As more tools adopt it, the protocol becomes more valuable to products. That feedback loop is what turns a collection of one-off integrations into an ecosystem.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Open integration protocols make one integration useful across many products. With bespoke connections, every AI product and tool provider has to build and maintain a separate connector for each pairing. A shared protocol lets a tool provider implement a common interface once and reach multiple compatible AI products. Each AI product that supports the protocol, in turn, can offer more tools without negotiating a partnership for every one.

That changes the incentive to participate. A small provider can reach users before it has the leverage to secure a partnership, and customers can switch AI products more easily while keeping the tools they rely on. Every new participant makes the ecosystem more useful to the others. That effect depends on reliable implementations and clear permission controls, since compatibility alone gives users little reason to trust a connection.
